title: The Manchester Baby: The First Machine to Actually Run a Stored Program (1948)
explainer: Built by Frederic Williams, Tom Kilburn, and Geoff Tootill mainly as a test of their new Williams-Kilburn memory tube, the Manchester Baby became, on 21 June 1948, the first machine to physically execute a program held in its own memory - running for about 52 minutes to find the highest factor of a number. It was deliberately tiny (32 words of memory) and not meant as a practical computer, but it closed the same gap you close in this capstone: turning a design that works on paper into physical logic gates and wires that actually run a program end to end. That distinguishes it from the stored-program concept itself (the earlier von Neumann design document) - this is about the first time the idea was soldered together and switched on.

resources.title: How a 70-year-old 'Baby' changed the face of modern computing
